newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN H1 seen boosted by dollar, U.S. buy.
newsitem.headline: ABN H1 seen boosted by dollar, U.S. buy.

text.p: Dutch bank ABN AMRO NV will underline the growing importance of its U.S. activities on Thursday when it unveils half year profits, expected to be at least 20 percent up on the same period a year ago.
Analysts said the higher U.S. dollar and acquisition of Standard Federal Bancorp would have made a significant impact on the operations of the bank in the first six months of 1997.
Forecasts of net profit range between 1.97 billion and 2.29 billion guilders ($1.1 billion), with an average estimate of 2.10 billion, up 23 percent on 1.7 billion guilders in the first half of 1996.
Analysts were also forecasting a dividend of 53 cents per share paid, up from 45 cents in the first half of 1996, adjusted for the recent four-for-one share split.

They said earnings from Michigan-based savings bank Standard Federal, bought for $1.95 billion and consolidated in ABN AMRO's accounts from January 1 this year, should have more than offset the sale of investment bank MeesPierson last year.
These deals increased the bank's reliance on interest income and reduced the importance of fees.
"They're benefiting from a lot of interest income in the U.S. The dollar will help that," said Peter Thorne of Paribas.
The dollar averaged about 1.90 guilders in the first half of 1997, compared with 1.67 a year earlier.
BZW analyst Heinie Hakker said the positive factors which made 1996 a record year for ABN AMRO had continued into 1997.
He cited strong growth in net interest income, commissions and trading income and, helped by an accounting change, falling loan loss provisioning.

"They have had a tremendous first half in terms of revenue growth," he said, adding that the bank may choose to smooth earnings by making more provisions for the adaptation of software for the euro currency and year 2000.
ABN had provided 340 million guilders for these projects by the end of 1996. But Dennis Ederzeel of Delta Lloyd Bank said: "There's not much room for more provisions."
He expected a 15 percent rise in net interest income, driven mainly by growth in lending in the Netherlands and the United States, its two main markets.
Ederzeel also assumed 55 percent growth in income from financial transactions, boosted by continued buoyancy in securities markets, particularly the Dutch sharemarket.
He added that forecasting trading income was notoriously difficult.
But other analysts were expecting slower growth or even a fall in trading income.
Income from financial transactions surged 86 percent in the first half of 1996, but the growth slowed in the second half, cutting the full-year increase to 57 percent.
Announcing its 1996 results in February, ABN AMRO declined to make a forecast about its current year performance because of the uncertainty in financial markets at the time.
